title: Where are you from?
goal: Say where you are from, where you live, and where a city is — and meet the first word endings that replace prepositions: *-s* and *-st*.
bekal: name countries, nationalities, and languages without mixing up their forms
use *-s* for "in" and *-st* for "from" on place names
know when a place takes *-l* instead of *-s* — a one-line rule that saves you

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kohvikus ülikooli juures
dialogs.intro: The next day, Kerli and Budi sit in a small café near the Tallinn University campus.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.id: Where exactly are you from, Budi?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bandung asub Jaava saarel. See on suur linn.
lines.id: Bandung is on the island of Java. It's a big city.
lines.literal: Bandung is-located-it Java island-on. it is big city.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Umbes kaks ja pool miljonit inimest.
lines.id: About two and a half million people.
lines.literal: about two and half million-(partial) person-(partial).

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Oi! Kogu Eestis elab ainult üks miljon inimest.
lines.id: Wow! In all of Estonia only one million people live.
lines.literal: wow! whole Estonia-in lives-it only one million person-(partial).

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tõesti? Ja sina, kust sa oled?
lines.id: Really? And you, where are you from?
lines.literal: really? and you, from-where you are-you?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ma olen Tartust, aga nüüd ma elan Tallinnas.
lines.id: I'm from Tartu, but now I live in Tallinn.
lines.literal: I am-I Tartu-from, but now I live-I Tallinn-in.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ei ole. Umbes kaks tundi bussiga.
lines.id: No. About two hours by bus.
lines.literal: no is-not. about two hour-(partial) bus-by.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja su pere? Kas nad elavad ka Tartus?
lines.id: And your family? Do they live in Tartu too?
lines.literal: and your family? is-it they live-they also Tartu-in?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.id: No, my parents live on Saaremaa.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Hea küsimus! Kohad, mis lõpevad -maa, võtavad -l.
lines.id: Good question! Places ending in -maa take -l.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Selge. Nii et Saksamaal ja Venemaal ka?
lines.id: I see. So Saksamaal and Venemaal too?
lines.literal: clear. so that Germany-on and Russia-on also?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Aitäh! Aga sina oled hea õpetaja.
lines.id: Thank you! But you really are a good teacher.
lines.literal: thank-you! but you are-you good teacher.

notes: **Indoneesiast, Bandungist, Tartust** — all place names + **-st**, meaning "from". Notice that this ending attaches directly, with no space, and the capital letter at the start of the name stays. English puts the preposition in front ("from Tartu"); Estonian glues it on the back. The meaning is the same.

**Tallinnas, Tartus, Eestis** — place names + **-s**, meaning "in". Pair it directly with *-st* from the previous note: *Tartus* (in Tartu) versus *Tartust* (from Tartu). The difference is one letter, and that letter is clearly audible.

**Su pere, mu vanemad.** *Su* is the short form of *sinu* (your), *mu* of *minu* (my). Just like *ma* and *mina* in Unit 1: the short one for ordinary conversation, the long one for emphasis. Possessives get full treatment in Unit 3.
⚠️ **Kui suur?** means "how big", not "if big". *Kui* has two jobs: in front of an adjective it means "how", elsewhere it means "if", "when", or "than". Context keeps them apart without difficulty.

grammars.title: Kus, kust, kuhu — three place questions
body: Estonian splits "where (at)", "where from", and "where to" into three different question words. English used to do the same (where / whence / whither), so this is a familiar idea — just three new words.
after: Notice that the answer ending **follows the question word**: *kus* calls for *-s*, *kust* calls for *-st*, *kuhu* calls for *-sse*. Once you catch this pairing, you don't need to memorize a table of cases — the question itself tells you which ending to use.
This unit works on the first two. *Kuhu* and *-sse* wait until Unit 7, because that's where the third length comes into play.

grammars.title: ⚠️ When a place takes -l instead of -s
body: Estonian has **two sets** of place endings. One means "inside", the other "on the surface". For ordinary objects the difference makes sense — *majas* (in the house) versus *laual* (on the table). For place names, the choice is fixed by tradition, and you simply follow it.

rows: ⚠️ Places ending in *-maa*, islands, and villages

after: The rule is one line: **if the place name ends in *-maa*, use *-l*.** *Saksamaal* (in Germany), *Venemaal* (in Russia), *Inglismaal* (in England), *Prantsusmaal* (in France), *Saaremaal* (on Saaremaa). Otherwise use *-s*: *Eestis*, *Soomes*, *Indoneesias*, *Jaapanis*, *Tallinnas*.
The reason happens to make sense: *maa* itself means "land", and people stand **on** land, not in it. English does something similar — we say "on land" and "on the ground", but "in the country".
A handful of exceptions will turn up later (*maal* itself means "in the countryside", *Hiiumaal*, *Vormsil*). Don't chase them now; the *-maa* rule already covers more than nine cases out of ten.

blocks.text: The first three columns of this table follow a very regular pattern: the country name, then **-lane** for the person, then the country name in its possessive form + *keel* for the language. Once you catch the pattern, you can guess rows you haven't seen yet.
⚠️ Look at the last four rows. The country ends in *-maa*, so its "in" form takes **-l**. Notice also that the nationality does **not** contain *-maa*: a German is *sakslane*, not "saksamaalane".

blocks.title: ⚠️ Three things that are easy to mix up
items: **Language names are always lowercase**, and always two words: *eesti keel*, not "Eesti keel". Country names keep their capital: *Eesti*.
**Nationalities are lowercase too**: *ta on eestlane*, not "Eestlane". This is the opposite of English, where "Estonian" gets a capital.
To say "I speak language X", the language takes the **partial** form: *ma räägin eesti keel**t***, *ma räägin inglise keel**t***. Memorize the ending as one package with the sentence.

blocks.title: Common place words
items: *linn* — city. *suur linn* = big city, *väike linn* = small city.
*küla* — village. *maa* — land, country, countryside. ⚠️ *maal* = "in the countryside", not "on land".
*saar* — island. *saarel* = on the island. Notice it takes *-l* too.
*riik* — state (as an institution). *pealinn* — capital city (literally: "head city").

rows: How long have you been in Estonia?

blocks.text: The last sentence uses a form you haven't learned yet (*mulle* = "to me"), but it is too useful to postpone. Memorize it whole: *mulle meeldib* + thing = "I like". Estonian says "to me X is pleasing", not "I like X" — a structure that will make sense once you reach Unit 16.
